sealed: Written and committed before src/keystore.mjs, src/trust.mjs, the command line's key care or tools/measure-4.mjs existed. Disclosed: designed after organ 3's page said keys are plain files with no passphrase, rotation or revocation, so a copied seed signs as its owner. tools/measure-4.mjs refuses to run if this file differs from the commit that sealed it. A claim that fails is kept.
what: Organ 4, key care. A private seed can be kept sealed under a passphrase: the passphrase stretched with PBKDF2-SHA-256 (600,000 iterations by default) into an AES-256-GCM key that encrypts the seed, with a fresh random salt and nonce, all through the platform's own WebCrypto so Node and a browser open a sealed key alike. Opening one with the wrong passphrase, or from a file changed in any way, is refused with its reason, never thrown. A trust list can carry revoked keys, each with a reason and a date; a bundle signed by a revoked key is refused and says it was revoked. Rotating a role makes a new key for it and revokes the old one. The command line seals keys when a passphrase is given (from an environment variable, so it never sits in the shell's history), signs only when the passphrase opens them, and can seal keys made earlier as plain files.
suite: 50 keys from fresh random seeds, each sealed at the default strength under its own passphrase. The tamper part changes every byte of the salt, the nonce and the sealed seed, the iteration count up and down, and the kind, of 5 of those keys re-sealed at 1,000 iterations, so it runs in CI in reasonable time: the strength changes how long a guess takes, not what the authentication tag checks, and the claim says so. Revocation runs over organ 3's 1,000 signed bundles and its demonstration keys. The command line runs end to end in a temporary folder.
scope: This protects a key at rest and lets a lost key be cut off. It does not protect a key while a passphrase-holder is using it, does not reach a hardware key (WebCrypto cannot), and a revocation acts only where the trust list that carries it is used. A bundle signed before a key was revoked is refused too: a signature carries no time a thief could not also write, so the record must be signed again by a key still trusted.

claims.claim: A sealed key holds no seed: for each of the 50 keys sealed at the default strength, no form of its seed (the raw bytes as text, hex, base64, base64url, or the PKCS#8 key in hex or base64) appears in the sealed file, and the file records 600,000 or more iterations.

Only the passphrase opens it: each of the 50 opens with its passphrase to a signer with the same public key as its seed; each of 3 wrong passphrases a key (150 tries) is refused; and on the 5 re-sealed keys, every one-byte change to the salt, the nonce or the sealed seed, the iteration count one up or one down, and a changed kind, is refused. None throws.

A revoked key cannot sign: over organ 3's 1,000 bundles, with nothing revoked every one verifies; with the recorder's key revoked, every one is refused and the refusal names the revocation; likewise with the judge's key revoked; with the reviewer's key revoked, every bundle carrying a review is refused; and revoking a key that signed none of them changes nothing.

Rotation cuts off the old key: for 100 of the 1,000 jobs, after the recorder's key is rotated, a bundle signed with the new key verifies under the rotated trust list, and a bundle signed afresh with the old key, as a thief holding its seed would, is refused as revoked.

The command line keeps no plain seed once a passphrase is given: acg keys with a passphrase writes no .seed file and no form of any seed anywhere under its folder; acg bundle with the right passphrase writes a bundle that verifies; with a wrong or missing passphrase it refuses, says why, and writes no bundle; and acg keys --seal turns plain seeds made earlier into sealed ones with the same public keys, leaving no plain seed behind.
